description:
I’m a PhD researcher in cancer biology with a background in bioengineering and an interest in science communication, education, and game design. I bring experience in scientific research, data analysis, and translating complex concepts into clear explanations.

I’m developing Outpost: MARS, a Mars habitat card game for children aged 7–12. Players balance resources like electricity, water, and crew time to complete mission objectives while responding to unexpected events.
summary:
Outpost: MARS is a browser-based card game that lets children aged 7–12 manage a Martian habitat. Across a mission lasting up to ten sols, players complete a lettuce growth study, deploy a rover, and install radiation shielding while balancing electricity, clean water, crew time, and wastewater storage. Unexpected dust storms, water leaks, and solar-particle events force players to reconsider their priorities.

The game addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning engineering trade-offs into decisions with visible consequences. Repairing solar panels takes time away from research; recycling water consumes electricity needed elsewhere. Every choice affects what becomes possible next.

The “Real Science” panels connect gameplay to NASA’s Curiosity imagery of the 2018 Martian dust storm and the 2024 solar particle event, with source credits and clear explanations of gameplay simplifications.

Outpost: MARS aims to make space science accessible through experimentation and replay. It encourages young learners to think about interconnected systems, plan ahead, and understand why maintaining a habitat matters as much as completing a mission.
details:
Outpost: MARS is an interactive browser game that introduces children aged 7–12 to the engineering decisions behind life on Mars. Players manage a small habitat and complete three objectives: conduct a lettuce growth study, deploy a rover, and install radiation shielding.

How it works

Each mission lasts up to ten turns, called sols. Players manage electricity, clean water, and crew time while keeping wastewater within the habitat’s storage capacity. A twelve-card deck contains action cards and unexpected events. Players begin with two cards and draw another card each sol, including the first.

Action cards offer opportunities such as backup power, more efficient work, or water recovery. Event cards activate the following sol, giving players a chance to prepare. Dust storms interrupt solar power generation, leaks drain clean water, and solar-particle events require completed shielding. Basic habitat actions remain available independently of the cards.

Players must weigh immediate progress against future needs. Repairing the solar array consumes time that could advance an objective. Recycling wastewater restores clean water but uses electricity. The mission ends successfully once all objectives are complete and the current sol’s upkeep is met.

NASA science and educational value

The “Real Science” panels connect decisions to relevant evidence. NASA’s Curiosity imagery of the June 2018 Martian dust storm illustrates changing atmospheric conditions, while imagery from the May 2024 solar particle event shows charged-particle effects on the rover’s camera detector. Players can access explanations through related cards and habitat systems.

Additional educational references include NASA’s information about Phobos and Deimos and Canadian Space Agency resources on growing crops. Sources are credited within the application. Historical observations and educational facts are clearly distinguished from simplified game rules; the prototype does not claim to predict radiation exposure or reproduce actual habitat performance.

Creativity and design choices

Outpost: MARS combines a card game with an interactive habitat. The habitat’s systems compete for shared resources, making engineering constraints part of the gameplay itself. Wastewater acts as an accumulating burden, encouraging players to consider storage and recycling alongside consumption.

The design prioritizes short instructions, recognizable resource icons, visible costs, and previews of what an action will leave behind. Illustrated cards, draw animations, and sound cues help communicate changes. Science explanations open on request, allowing players to explore the evidence without spending game resources.

Tools and development

The application was developed and published using Base44, with ChatGPT assisting in gameplay design, prompt preparation, and explanatory text. The browser interface uses JavaScript-based interactions and procedural WebAudio ambience and sound effects. NASA imagery is bundled into the prototype, so these educational features do not require a live NASA API connection. Players need a web browser and no specialist hardware.

Intended impact and next steps

Outpost: MARS aims to encourage planning, curiosity, and systems thinking by letting learners experience the consequences of competing priorities. It could support independent exploration or classroom discussions about resource management and space exploration.

Learning outcomes have not yet been evaluated with children. The next step is supervised playtesting to assess whether players can explain the trade-offs they encountered, followed by improvements to instructions, accessibility, and difficulty.
